hook: You know Revelation 3:20, Jesus knocking at the door. But did you know the door belongs to a church?
story:
In 1851 the English painter William Holman Hunt began a picture that would travel the world. It shows Jesus about to knock on a door that has not been opened for a long time. Weeds have grown up against it. Look closely and you see what Hunt intended: there is no handle on the outside. This door opens only from within.

He called it The Light of the World. When a later version toured the world between 1905 and 1907, crowds came to stand in front of it. It hangs today in St Paul’s Cathedral in London.

The painting made this verse a picture of Christ at the door of a single heart, and it has spoken to many people that way. The letter itself holds one more surprise. The door belongs to a church. The people inside already carry his name. They are comfortable, and sure they need nothing. And he is standing outside, knocking.

Cru: Would You Like to Know God Personally?

moment:
The speaker is the risen Jesus, who introduces himself here as “the Faithful and True Witness”. He is sending seven letters to seven churches, and this is the last of them, to “the assembly in Laodicea”.

It is one of the sternest of the seven. The church thinks it is doing well: “I am rich, and have gotten riches, and have need of nothing”. He tells them the truth they cannot see. And then the tone turns in a single line: “As many as I love, I reprove and chasten.” The knock at the door comes from someone who has not given up on them.
around: The verse before it sets the tone: “As many as I love, I reprove and chasten. Be zealous therefore, and repent.” The knock is part of that correction, and it comes with a promise to come in and eat with anyone who opens.
readings:
Preachers have long used this verse to invite people to faith: Christ stands at the door of every heart and waits to be let in. Hunt’s painting fixed that picture in many minds.

Readers who stay with the letter notice that the invitation is first addressed to believers. On this reading the verse is about renewal. A church, or a Christian, can go on with the routines of faith while Christ himself has been left outside.

And many have noticed the meal. He promises to come in and eat with anyone who opens. Some hear in that the fellowship of the Lord’s table, and some the great feast at the end of all things. Either way, the knock ends at a shared table.
argued:
In 1874, preaching in London on the letter to Laodicea, Charles Spurgeon said he had often heard this text preached to unbelievers, as if Christ were knocking at their door. He disagreed: [[spurgeon-rev]]

In the next century the other reading went around the world. Cru, the ministry founded by Bill and Vonette Bright, developed the Four Spiritual Laws in 1957, and more than two and a half billion copies of the booklet have been printed. One of its principles is that a person receives Christ by personal invitation, and Cru’s own page still explains it with this verse.

One verse, two doors: the door of a single heart, and the door of a church that has left its Lord outside. Both readings are still preached today.
point: The picture is of Christ outside a congregation that carries his name, asking to be let back in. Many Christians also use the verse when inviting someone to faith. In Revelation it is first a call to a church to repent.
